safety_verdicts.content: The patient initially experienced a weird sensation around the lips.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Gold notes an initial weird sensation around the lips; generated facts do not mention this prodromal ‘weird feeling’.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Omitting the initial “weird sensation” around the lips removes a minor prodromal detail but does not materially change recognition or management of the acute allergic reaction already described (lip swelling and breathing symptoms). Clinical decision-making and urgency would be driven by the airway/respiratory complaints rather than this early sensation.

safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Gold states the patient feels dizzy; no dizziness is captured in the generated facts.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Dizziness can be a marker of systemic involvement (e.g., hypotension/presyncope) in anaphylaxis, and failing to document it could reduce perceived severity and affect triage/monitoring decisions. While the encounter still resulted in emergency escalation, this omission could contribute to underestimation of risk in downstream documentation.

safety_verdicts.content: During consultation, the patient appeared to have breathing difficulties.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Gold includes clinician-observed breathing difficulty during the consultation; generated facts only record reported symptoms and do not document this as an observed physical finding.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Not documenting clinician-observed breathing difficulty is higher risk because it is a red-flag feature supporting anaphylaxis/impending airway compromise and may influence urgency, disposition, and need for epinephrine. Downstream clinicians relying on the note could underestimate the acuity if only patient-reported symptoms are captured.

safety_verdicts.content: Examination showed progressively increasing lip swelling.

Omitting this observed progression could lead to under-triage or less aggressive monitoring/treatment planning.
